practice: Write an opening sentence using a metaphor for the sea.
Add one sentence with two senses (not sight).
Rewrite 'The sky was grey' using a simile or personification.
independent: Core: Write the first paragraph of a description for the pier prompt (80 words).
Extend: Write three paragraphs that move from wide to detail to wide, using at least three senses.
Stretch: Write a 300-word description with a deliberate shift in tone and a final echo of the opening.
exit: Name two ways to give a description structure.
Rewrite 'It was cold' with a precise image.
Big question: how can I make a reader see without telling them what to feel?
lessons.homework: Describe in 120 words the view from your window at an unusual time of day, using at least three senses and one simile.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a four-box camera planner and a word bank (weathered, shuttered, stubborn, pewter). EAL/international: pre-teach 'pier', 'arcade', 'out of season', 'weathered', 'shuttered'; idiom 'the calm before the storm' = quiet just before trouble; stems: 'In the distance there was ...', 'The air smelled of ...', 'It looked as if ...'. Cultural note: seaside holiday towns and piers, winter closures. Stretch: write in the second person to alter the viewpoint.

lessons.unit: P1-B-Q5: Paper 1 Section B: Question 5, descriptive or narrative writing
lessons.title: Question 5: narrative writing with a controlled structure
lessons.bigQuestion: How do I shape a short story so that it feels complete in 40 minutes?
objectives: Plan a short narrative with one focus and a clear ending
Open and close a story with deliberate effect
Use dialogue, thought and pace to show character rather than explain it
successCriteria: All: write a story with an opening, a problem and an ending
Most: control pace, using sentence length and paragraphs
Some: echo a motif from the beginning at the end to create shape

keywords.def: a story or account of events
an image or idea that is repeated
spoken words between characters
a scene from an earlier time
the way the problem is dealt with at the end

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: name the four stages of the camera plan from the last lesson.
Write an opening sentence that starts in the middle of an action.
Define 'cliffhanger'.

teach.heading: The task
bullets: Task: a story about a moment of waiting for news.
Choose: one place, one character, one problem.
Write about 450-600 words in 30 minutes.
Plan for five minutes; check for five.
teach.note: Task: 'Write a story about a moment when someone is waiting for news.' (40 marks). Remind pupils that Paper 1 Section B has one task, either descriptive or narrative; pupils choose the one they can do best. Cultural context: in the UK, news may arrive by phone, letter or doorbell; any culture's version is welcome.

teach.heading: A five-point plan

timeline.label: 1. Open
timeline.text: start in the moment, with a precise detail (the motif)

timeline.label: 2. Build
timeline.text: show waiting: time, small actions, thoughts

timeline.label: 3. Twist
timeline.text: a sound, a message or a decision changes things

timeline.label: 4. Climax
timeline.text: the news arrives, in few words

timeline.label: 5. Close
timeline.text: echo the motif; end with a feeling or image

teach.note: Say that short stories do not cover long periods. A tight timeline gives control. Ask pupils to pick an unusual starting point (the news just arrived, or an object on a table). Introduce a motif as the 'thread' to link the opening to the ending.

teach.heading: Worked model: opening and ending

model.problem: Write the opening and the ending of a story about a moment of waiting for news.
steps: Opening: start with a concrete motif, the kettle, and a time.
Show the waiting through small actions rather than saying 'she was nervous'.
Ending: bring back the kettle, but changed by what has happened.
Keep the final sentence short.
model.answer: OPENING: The kettle clicked off for the third time, and still Nadia did not pour. The phone lay face down on the table like a card she was afraid to turn over. ... ENDING: The phone rang. She listened; she said, 'Yes. Yes. Thank you.' Then she lifted the kettle, and for the first time that day her hands were steady.

teach.note: Note that the motif of the kettle returns at the end with a changed meaning. Also note that the opening starts in the moment and the ending is short. Ask: what has changed in the final kettle? Draw out that repetition with a difference gives shape.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which opening is strongest for this task?
options: The kettle clicked off for the third time, and still Nadia did not pour.
Nadia was very nervous and could not wait any longer for the news.
On Monday Nadia woke up, had breakfast, went to school and then waited.
check.why: A begins in the moment with a concrete motif and implies tension. B tells the emotion; C lists a day and loses focus.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is A; C tells emotions; B is a list of events rather than a moment.

teach.heading: Dialogue and punctuation

misconception.wrong: "I am waiting" said Nadia, "for the call." She said it nervous.
misconception.right: "I'm waiting for the call," said Nadia, her fingers tight round the mug.

teach.note: Say direct speech needs a new line for each speaker and accurate punctuation. Idiom: 'to be on edge' = to be tense and nervous.

practice: Choose a motif and write your opening sentence.
Write three sentences showing waiting through small actions only.
Write the closing sentence using the same motif with a changed meaning.
independent: Core: Write the opening and ending paragraphs for the task.
Extend: Write the full story in four paragraphs with the five-point plan.
Stretch: Rewrite your story using a flashback in paragraph two and explain the effect.
exit: Name the five stages of the plan.
What is a motif and why is it useful?
Big question: how do I make a short story feel complete?
lessons.homework: Write a 200-word story ending that echoes an object introduced at the opening, then annotate where it returns.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a plan template with five numbered boxes and a bank of 'small actions' (tapping, pacing, checking). EAL/international: pre-teach 'motif', 'kettle', 'steady', 'on edge', 'echo'; idiom 'to hold your breath' = to wait anxiously; stems: 'She could not stop ...', 'The silence seemed ...', 'At last, ...'. Cultural note: a kettle and tea are common in UK homes at stressful moments; use any familiar object. Stretch: write in first person present tense and keep it consistent.

lessons.unit: SC-W: Subject content: writing across the course
lessons.title: Writing for different purposes: explain, instruct, inform, argue
lessons.bigQuestion: How does my purpose change the way I write the same topic?
objectives: Name the writing purposes in the GCSE range: describe, narrate, explain, instruct, inform, argue
Match features of language and structure to each purpose
Adapt one topic for two purposes and two audiences
successCriteria: All: name the purpose of a text
Most: choose features that suit the purpose
Some: rewrite the same content for a new purpose and audience with controlled register
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: instructions and explanations in practical reports
lessons.smsc: Social: communicating respectfully with different audiences

keywords.def: what the writer wants the text to do
the people the text is written for
the level of formality in language
a command verb used for instructions
a question asked for effect, not for an answer

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: name the three things stated before every Paper 2 Question 5 (audience, purpose and ...).
Write a sentence giving an instruction.
Is 'Hey guys, check this out' formal or informal?

teach.heading: Six purposes

head: Purpose
Typical features
Example opening
rows: On the day the letter came ...

teach.note: Say the specification names these six purposes; pupils should be able to write in all. Ask pupils to give a real-world example of each (recipe, news, letter). For EAL pupils, say we still expect Standard English whatever the accent or first language.

teach.heading: Same topic, two purposes

left.title: Inform (for parents)
points: The canteen serves hot meals from 12.00 to 1.00.
A main course costs £2.50.
Vegetarian and halal options are offered daily.

right.title: Argue (to the headteacher)
points: Surely every pupil deserves a hot lunch that is affordable.
At £2.50, a meal is too expensive for many families.
We must act now to provide free lunches.

teach.note: Show that the topic 'school lunch' can be informing or arguing. Ask pupils to notice register, fact versus opinion and sentence forms. Point out that audience (headteacher or pupils) changes vocabulary too.

teach.heading: Worked model: adapting a paragraph

model.problem: Rewrite this informative sentence for an argument to the headteacher: 'The school library closes at 3.30.'
steps: Identify the facts: the library, the time 3.30.
Add a stance: closing early harms pupils.
Add a persuasive device: a rhetorical question or a triplet.
Adjust register: formal but forceful.
model.answer: Surely a school that values reading should not lock its library at 3.30, just when pupils have time to read, research and revise? Closing early denies the children who need it most a quiet place to learn.

teach.note: Model the rewrite step by step: keep facts, change features. Ask where the register moves from neutral to persuasive. Say that using the same facts in both texts shows that the purpose changes the choices.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which sentence argues rather than informs?
options: First, wash your hands for twenty seconds.
Surely every community deserves a library that is open when people can use it.
check.why: C uses an opinion and a rhetorical question. A is an instruction; B is a neutral fact.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is C. A uses imperatives (instruct); B informs.

teach.heading: Audience and register
bullets: Friend: informal, contractions, humour.
Headteacher: formal, full sentences, polite.
Younger children: simple words, short sentences.
Newspaper readers: clear, engaging, balanced.
teach.note: Say: the same writer changes tone for a friend and for a head teacher. Idiom: 'to strike the right note' = to use the correct tone.

practice: Write one sentence for each of these purposes about a school trip: inform, instruct, argue.
Rewrite 'You must be quiet!' for a polite note to a neighbour.
Choose the purpose for each text: a recipe, a leaflet about flu jabs, a letter to the council.
independent: Core: Write 60 words to inform parents about a school trip, then 60 words to argue for it.
Extend: Rewrite the argument paragraph for pupils aged 8, changing register.
Stretch: Write a 150-word explanation of how a rainbow forms, then describe it in a poetic paragraph; compare your choices.
exit: Name the six purposes.
Which feature is typical of instruction?
Big question: how does purpose change my writing?
lessons.homework: Write a 100-word instruction on making tea and a 100-word argument for why everyone should learn to cook; underline three differences.
lessons.send: SEND: give a purpose-feature matching card sort and a sentence frame for each purpose. EAL/international: pre-teach 'purpose', 'audience', 'register', 'imperative'; idioms 'to strike the right note', 'to put it bluntly'; stems: 'First, ...', 'Because ..., therefore ...', 'It is clear that ...'. Cultural note: British letters often open 'Dear Sir or Madam' and close 'Yours faithfully' when the name is unknown; 'Yours sincerely' when it is known. Stretch: write the same paragraph in three registers.

lessons.unit: SC-W: Subject content: writing across the course
lessons.title: Standard English, grammar and punctuation for technical accuracy
lessons.bigQuestion: How can accurate writing add marks without making my writing dull?
objectives: Use Standard English grammar in formal writing
Punctuate complex sentences, avoiding comma splices
Vary sentence structures for effect
successCriteria: All: write in complete sentences with capital letters and full stops
Most: use commas, apostrophes and semi-colons correctly
Some: vary sentence openings and lengths deliberately for effect
lessons.crossCurricular: MFL and Arabic: comparing sentence structures across languages
lessons.smsc: Social: respect for different dialects while using Standard English where needed

keywords.def: the grammar and vocabulary used in formal writing across the UK, not an accent
two main clauses wrongly joined by only a comma
joins two closely linked main clauses
shows possession or missing letters
the verb matches the subject: they were, not they was

starter: Bismillah. Retrieval: what is the difference between a main clause and a subordinate clause?
Correct: 'We was late for school'.
Add a full stop and capital letter to: it was raining we stayed in.

teach.heading: Standard English: grammar, not accent
teach.note: Say clearly: Standard English is about grammar and vocabulary, not accent; every accent is welcome. Dialect or non-standard forms may appear in dialogue for effect, but narration and formal writing use Standard English. For international pupils, note that some forms (we was, I done it) are common in speech around the UK but not in exam writing.

teach.heading: Fix the comma splice

left.title: Comma splice (wrong)
points: The sea was calm, the boats stayed in the harbour.
I was tired, I kept writing.

right.title: Fixed (right)
points: The sea was calm; the boats stayed in the harbour.
I was tired, but I kept writing.
I was tired. I kept writing.

teach.note: Show three fixes: full stop, semi-colon, conjunction. Ask pupils to decide which gives the best rhythm. Point out that fixing is easy once you spot two complete sentences.

teach.heading: Worked model: upgrading a paragraph

model.problem: Improve this paragraph for technical accuracy and variety: 'it was dark we walked home. we was cold. the streetlights was flickering the road was wet.'
steps: Fix capitals and full stops.
Correct 'we was' and 'the streetlights was'.
Split or join the comma splice with a semi-colon or conjunction.
Vary the openings and add one short sentence.
model.answer: It was dark when we walked home. We were cold. The streetlights were flickering; the road was wet and shone like black glass. Nobody spoke.

teach.note: Read the draft aloud, then the model. Ask pupils to count the techniques added: variety of openings, a semi-colon, a participle phrase, a short sentence. Emphasise accuracy as well as variety.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The rain stopped, we went out.
The rain stopped; we went out.
The rain stopped we went out.
check.why: B uses a semi-colon to join two linked main clauses. A is a comma splice; C has no punctuation at all.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. The answer is B. A is a splice; C is non-standard.

teach.heading: Apostrophes at a glance

misconception.wrong: The dog wagged it's tail, and the childrens' coats were wet.
misconception.right: The dog wagged its tail, and the children's coats were wet.

teach.note: Run a quick quiz. Remind pupils: its (belonging) versus it's (it is).

Fix three comma splices in three different ways.
Write one sentence with a semi-colon and one with a participle opening.

exit: Is Standard English an accent? Explain.
Fix: 'It was late, we went home.'

teach.heading: Text C: A Night in the Dunes
teach.note: Teacher-written travel writing. Read twice: once for meaning, once with a pen.

quote.text: By the time we reached the dunes, the heat had drained from the sand like water from a basin. Our guide said nothing; he simply pointed upward. I have seen city skies and mountain skies, but nothing prepared me for this: a sky so crowded with stars that the darkness seemed the exception.

teach.heading: Model: explicit then implicit
teach.note: Think aloud.

model.problem: What does the guide's silence suggest?
steps: Explicit: 'Our guide said nothing'
Clue: he 'simply pointed upward'
Inference: the view needs no words; he knows it is extraordinary
Write: Point + brief quotation + inference
model.answer: The guide's silence ('said nothing') implies the sky is so remarkable that words would only diminish it.

teach.heading: Hinge
teach.note: Poll.

check.q: Which is an inference rather than retrieval?
options: The heat drained from the sand.
The writer is used to busy, light-polluted places.
check.why: It is not stated; it is drawn from 'city skies' and 'the darkness seemed the exception'.

practice.q: Retrieve two things the writer has seen before.
practice.a: City skies and mountain skies.
practice.model: Find the sentence starting 'I have seen'. Copy only the two items: city skies, mountain skies.

practice.q: Infer how the writer feels about this sky, with one word as evidence.
practice.a: Overwhelmed or amazed: 'nothing prepared me'.

independent.q: Core: answer the six questions on Text C on the pupil PDF (four retrieval, two inference with a short quotation each).
independent.a: Retrieval: dunes, heat drained, guide pointed, crowded with stars. Inference: guide's familiarity and respect; writer's sense of wonder.
independent.model: Inference question model: 'What does "crowded with stars" suggest?' Answer: It suggests an overwhelming number of stars, so many that the sky feels full, showing the writer's astonishment.

independent.q: Extend: write one sentence explaining the difference between your retrieval and inference answers.
independent.a: Retrieval states what the text says; inference explains what it suggests.

independent.q: Stretch: infer something about the writer's normal life.
independent.a: He or she usually lives in a city with light pollution and finds rare peace here.

exit.q: Answer the ponder: how can a writer say something without saying it?
exit.a: Through actions, silences and word choices that the reader interprets.

lessons.homework: Read a short travel article and write two explicit details and one inference.
lessons.send: SEND: Text C with key lines highlighted; answer frames. EAL: glossary (dunes, basin, exception). Stretch: infer the guide's attitude to the desert.

successCriteria: All: identify a language method and its effect
Most: zoom in on the connotations of a single word

keywords.def: ideas and feelings a word suggests
a comparison using like or as
how the language makes the reader think or feel
correct names for methods

hook.text: Is it enough to say 'the writer uses a simile'? What would a reader actually want to know?

teach.heading: Effect first
teach.note: Compare the two.

misconception.wrong: The writer uses a simile, 'like water from a basin', which is effective.
misconception.right: The heat vanishes suddenly and completely, 'like water from a basin', so the desert seems to change in an instant.

teach.heading: Zooming in
bullets: Choose one word: 'drained'
Connotations: emptied, gone, exhausted
Effect: the desert loses its fierce heat
Then name the method
teach.note: Model on the mini-whiteboard.

teach.heading: Model: PETZAAL with effect leading
teach.note: Labelled.

model.problem: How does the writer use language to show the desert at night?
steps: Point: the writer presents the night as a sudden transformation.
Evidence: 'the heat had drained from the sand like water from a basin'
Technique: simile
Zoom: 'drained' suggests emptying completely
Analyse: the fierce day vanishes, leaving calm
Link: language makes the change feel instant
model.answer: A PETZAAL paragraph.

teach.heading: Hinge
teach.note: Poll.

check.q: Which sentence lets effect lead?
options: The sky seems alive and crowded, as if the stars are pushing the darkness aside.
check.why: It explains the reader's impression first; terminology can follow.

practice.q: Zoom in on 'crowded': two connotations and the effect.
practice.a: Busy, full; the sky feels packed with stars, overwhelming the writer.
practice.model: Word: crowded. Connotations: full, busy, pushing. Effect: abundance, almost noisy, which contrasts with the silence.

practice.q: Rewrite with effect first: 'The writer uses a colon.'
practice.a: The pause before 'a sky so crowded' builds anticipation, then reveals the view (colon).

independent.q: Core: write a PETZAAL paragraph in the portal response box: 'How does the writer use language to present the night sky?' Starter: 'The writer presents the night sky as...'
independent.a: A PETZAAL paragraph where effect leads and terminology supports.
independent.model: Point: The writer presents the night sky as overwhelming in its beauty. | Evidence: 'a sky so crowded with stars that the darkness seemed the exception' | Technique: hyperbole and inversion of expectation | Zoom in: 'exception' reverses the normal idea that night is dark. | Analyse: The reader shares the writer's astonishment at a sky where light, not dark, is normal. | Alternative: It could also suggest how much the writer has been missing in brightly lit cities. | Link: So language makes the sky feel like a revelation.

independent.q: Extend: add a second short paragraph on the guide.
independent.a: Analysis of 'said nothing' or 'simply'.

independent.q: Stretch: check that every method you name is followed by its effect.
independent.a: All methods explained.

exit.a: No: readers want to know what the method does and why it matters.

lessons.homework: Find one simile or metaphor in a news article and write an effect-led sentence about it.
lessons.send: SEND: zoom-in grid. EAL: method glossary. Stretch: analyse sentence form too.

lessons.unit: P1-A-Q4: Paper 1 Section A: Question 4, evaluation
lessons.title: Question 4: agree or disagree, because the quality of evaluation earns the marks
lessons.bigQuestion: If I disagree with the statement, will I lose marks?
objectives: Understand that marks reward the quality of evaluation, not the position taken
Build a balanced evaluative judgement with evidence
Use evaluative stems to reach a justified view
successCriteria: All: state an opinion and support it with one quotation
Most: explain how the writer creates the effect and why you judge it as you do
Some: weigh up the statement and give a measured conclusion
lessons.crossCurricular: Citizenship: forming and justifying a reasoned opinion
lessons.smsc: Moral: fairness in weighing evidence, even when you disagree

keywords.def: judge how successful something is, using evidence
the opinion about the text printed in the question
how far you agree
give reasons and evidence for a view

starter: Bismillah. Complete: 'I partly agree because ...' about the statement 'Homework should be banned.'
Define 'evaluate' in your own words.
Retrieval: how many marks is Paper 1 Question 4?

teach.heading: What Question 4 really tests
bullets: A statement about the text is printed in the question
You judge how far you agree, citing evidence
The question carries 20 marks
Evaluation is marked on quality, not on which side you pick
teach.note: State the key point twice: you cannot 'fail' by disagreeing. A pupil who disagrees with strong evidence and explanation will score as highly as one who agrees. Ask: why would examiners design it this way? (Because AO4 is about critical judgement.) The statement usually focuses on a part of the text, so pupils should stay within the lines given.

teach.heading: The extract and statement

quote.text: Statement: 'The writer makes Maya seem very brave.' Evidence from the extract: She walked towards the black water, though her hands were trembling. 'I am not afraid,' she whispered, and did not believe a word of it.
quote.source: Original extract and statement written for TGA

teach.note: Read together. Elicit initial gut reactions: agree, disagree or partly. Emphasise that both brave (she walks forward) and afraid (trembling, whispered) are in the same lines, so strong answers can use both.

teach.heading: Model: two high-quality answers, opposite views

left.title: Agree (mostly)
points: 'she walked towards the black water' shows decisive action
The determination is clear even while 'her hands were trembling'
Bravery here means acting despite fear

right.title: Disagree (partly)
points: 'did not believe a word of it' shows Maya lies to herself
'whispered' suggests she lacks confidence
She seems frightened, so brave is too simple

teach.note: Both positions can reach the top level because each uses precise quotation, explains how the writer creates the impression and gives a reasoned judgement. Ask pupils to find the strongest piece of evidence on each side. Emphasise 'to what extent' invites a nuanced view in the middle.

teach.heading: Worked paragraph

model.problem: 'The writer makes Maya seem very brave.' To what extent do you agree? (20 marks, one paragraph)
steps: State your view clearly and with a degree: 'I partly agree.'
Choose a quotation that supports it and explain the writer's method.
Choose a quotation that complicates it and explain the effect.
Reach a judgement that weighs the two.
model.answer: I partly agree that Maya seems brave. She 'walked towards the black water', and the verb 'walked' shows she is moving forward, not running away. However, the writer undercuts this with 'her hands were trembling', which makes her fear physical and visible. The final clause, 'did not believe a word of it', shows she is trying to persuade herself, so her bravery seems effortful rather than natural. Overall, the writer presents courage as acting despite fear, which makes Maya more convincing and human than a fearless hero.

teach.note: Highlight the sequence: view, evidence, method, effect, weighing, judgement. Ask: where does it say 'I agree' or 'I disagree'? Only once, at the start. The rest is evaluation. Praise a model that changes mind within the paragraph, because that is critical.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: A pupil strongly disagrees with the statement and gives three well-explained quotations. What is the best prediction of their mark?
options: Low, because the statement should be supported
High, because the evaluation is strong
Impossible to tell until you check the position
check.why: Marks are for the quality of the evaluation. Disagreement is fully acceptable if supported by evidence and analysis.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. If some pick A, ask: what would the examiner be rewarding? Redirect to the quality of evaluation: evidence, method, effect, judgement.

practice: Write a one-sentence view on the statement, using a degree such as 'partly', 'mostly' or 'completely'.
Select the best quotation to oppose your view and say what it suggests.
Finish: 'Overall, the writer presents Maya as ... because ...'
independent: Core: Write a four-sentence evaluative paragraph that agrees partly.
Extend: Write a second paragraph that argues the opposite view, using different quotations.
Stretch: Write a conclusion that explains why neither view is complete, linking to the writer's purpose.
exit: True or false: you must agree with the statement to score highly.
Write one sentence beginning 'I partly agree because ...'.
Big question: how is the position you take marked?
lessons.homework: Take a statement about a character in a book you know, for example 'The writer makes the hero seem selfish'. Write one paragraph arguing for, and one against, then decide which you prefer.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a sentence-starter card ('I agree because ...', 'However ...', 'This shows ...'). EAL/international: pre-teach 'undercut', 'trembling', 'determination', 'convincing'; allow a bilingual vocabulary list. Stretch: write one paragraph which changes position half way and explain why the change is valid.

lessons.unit: P1-B-Q5: Paper 1 Section B: Question 5, descriptive or narrative writing
lessons.title: Question 5: choosing your task, and controlling tone, style, register and cohesion
lessons.bigQuestion: How do I make my writing sound right for the task and hold together from start to finish?
objectives: Choose between describing and narrating from the written prompt or image given
Control tone, style and register for the stated audience and purpose
Organise paragraphs so that the piece is coherent and cohesive
successCriteria: All: choose a task and keep one consistent tone
Most: use connectives and links that guide the reader
Some: shape tone, register and structure deliberately for effect
lessons.crossCurricular: Art: composition and the viewer's eye
lessons.smsc: Cultural: seeing everyday scenes with fresh eyes

keywords.def: the attitude or mood of the writing
how formal or informal the language is
the piece makes sense as a whole
ideas are linked smoothly between sentences and paragraphs
a story; description paints a picture

starter: Bismillah. Name one feature of descriptive writing and one of narrative writing.
Is 'It was proper rubbish' formal or informal?
Retrieval: how many marks are given for content and organisation in Question 5?

teach.heading: One extended task
bullets: Question 5 is one extended task of 40 marks
Choose to describe or narrate, from a prompt or an image
The statement before the task sets audience and purpose
Commit to your choice within the first two minutes
teach.note: AQA offers a choice of tasks; check the specimen paper for the exact layout this year (verify). Stress that either option can reach the top marks. Ask who prefers images and who prefers words, then discuss strengths. Note that 24 marks are for content and organisation and 16 for technical accuracy.

teach.heading: Tone, style and register

head: Feature
What it means
Example
rows: Your choices of words and sentences
Short blunt sentences or flowing ones

teach.note: Show how the same moment changes with tone: 'The train left.' versus 'The train slipped away, leaving silence on the platform.' Ask: which register suits a magazine competition entry? Stress consistency; avoid slipping into slang unless dialogue calls for it.

teach.heading: Coherence and cohesion
cycle: Open with a clear scene or situation
Link each paragraph to the last (time, place, contrast)
Develop one idea per paragraph
Return to an image or motif at the end
teach.note: Coherence is the whole piece making sense; cohesion is the stitching between sentences. Model discourse markers such as 'Meanwhile', 'Moments later', 'Beyond the window'. Warn against starting every paragraph with 'Then'. A circular structure (return to the opening image) delivers cohesion.

teach.heading: Model: a tightly controlled opening

model.problem: Write the opening of a description of a railway station at dusk (audience: a school magazine). Use a calm, observant tone and formal-neutral register.
steps: Open with a precise setting detail rather than 'It was a station'.
Use one controlled metaphor and one sensory detail.
Vary sentence length and keep the tone steady.
End the paragraph with a link that leads to the next idea.
model.answer: Dusk settled over the station like a grey blanket. Beneath the clock, a lone porter swept the same square of platform, patient as a metronome. The air smelled of cold iron and damp coats. Somewhere beyond the signal lamps, a train was breathing its way towards us. And yet nobody looked up.

teach.note: Read it twice. Ask pupils to identify tone (calm, observant), register (formal-neutral) and the linking device ('And yet'). Stress that the standard is not long words but controlled, deliberate choices. Original model written for TGA.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which sentence breaks the register of a calm magazine description?
options: The porter swept patiently beneath the clock.
The platform was totally mega boring, mate.
check.why: B slides into slang that clashes with the controlled, formal-neutral tone. A and C fit.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. If pupils pick A or C, ask them to say what tone each sentence achieves.

practice: Rewrite 'The sky was dark and I was scared' in a formal-neutral register with one metaphor.
Add a linking phrase to join these: 'The hall was silent.' 'A door opened.'
Choose a task (description or narrative) and write its first sentence with a clear tone.
independent: Core: Write a five-sentence description of a street at dawn, keeping one tone.
Extend: Add two different linking devices and underline them.
Stretch: Write two openings of the same scene in two contrasting tones and explain how register shifts.
exit: Define 'register' in your own words.
Write one linking phrase you could use between paragraphs.
Big question: how do tone and linking help your writing sound controlled?
lessons.homework: Choose one of the Question 5 tasks from your specimen paper. Plan it in five bullet points, naming your tone, register and the three links between paragraphs.
lessons.send: SEND: give a paragraph frame and a link-words mat. EAL/international: pre-teach 'dusk', 'porter', 'metronome', 'signal lamps'; model the distinction between formal and informal with a two-column list. Stretch: write an extra paragraph that deliberately shifts tone and justify the shift.

lessons.unit: P1-B-Q5: Paper 1 Section B: Question 5, descriptive or narrative writing
lessons.title: Question 5: managing your time across the 1 hour 45 minute paper
lessons.bigQuestion: How should I spend my 105 minutes so that Question 5 gets the time it deserves?
objectives: Know the paper's length and the notional reading time included in it
Plan a realistic timing budget for each question
Reserve time at the end to check writing for accuracy
successCriteria: All: state the total time and where reading time sits
Most: build a timing plan that adds up to 105 minutes
Some: adapt the plan after a slow start without losing time for Question 5
lessons.smsc: Moral: responsibility and self-discipline in using time well

keywords.def: counted as a guide rather than strictly timed
a budget of minutes for each task
read through to find and fix errors

starter: Bismillah. How many minutes are in 1 hour 45 minutes?
List the five Paper 1 questions with their marks.
Retrieval: name two things to check in your Question 5 writing.

teach.heading: The paper in numbers
teach.note: Total: 105 minutes. Say that AQA builds a notional 15 minutes of reading time into the 1 hour 45 minutes; it is not separate time. The timings are guidance (approx.): verify against the paper's front cover and your specimen. Ask: why does Q5 get the longest slot? (40 of 80 marks.)

teach.heading: A timeline for Question 5

timeline.label: 5 to 40 min
timeline.text: Write in a controlled, organised way

teach.note: Model the plan: choose, plan, write, check. Warn against spending twenty minutes planning. Note that technical accuracy accounts for 16 marks, so the five-minute check is worth real marks. Use the idea of ihsan: doing a task with care and excellence.

teach.heading: Model: adapting when you overrun

model.problem: You have 30 minutes left but have only just started Question 5. What do you do?
steps: Stay calm and spend two minutes on a brief plan.
Shorten the piece: aim for a clear beginning, middle and end.
Write confidently; do not restart.
Leave the last three minutes for checking spelling and punctuation.
model.answer: Plan for 2 minutes, write for 25, check for 3. A shorter, controlled piece with accurate punctuation will score better than an unfinished ambitious one.

teach.note: Emphasise that panic wastes more time than a shorter piece. Ask pupils what they would cut: extra description, a second flashback, an overlong ending.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Why is checking time built into the plan?
options: It protects marks for spelling, punctuation and sentence control
check.why: Technical accuracy is worth 16 of the 40 marks, so a short check recovers marks cheaply.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. Revisit 16 versus 24 marks.

teach.heading: Common error

misconception.wrong: 'I will use the 15 minutes of reading time as extra thinking time before I start writing.'
misconception.right: The 15 minutes is notional and already inside the 1 hour 45 minutes. Use it for reading the extract, then keep moving.

teach.note: Clarify that the paper is one continuous 1 hour 45 minutes. The 15 minutes is a recommended share, not extra time. Ask pupils to underline it on their timing plan.

practice: Add: 15 + 5 + 10 + 10 + 20 + 45. What do you get?
Adjust the plan for a student who spends 25 minutes on Question 4.
Write the three steps of your Question 5 timeline in your own words.
independent: Core: Create your own timing plan for Paper 1 on a small card.
Extend: Write a Question 5 title, plan it in 5 minutes using a timer.
Stretch: Write a short paragraph explaining how you would adapt the plan if you were slow on Question 2.
exit: How long is Paper 1, and what part is notional reading time?
How many minutes would you give to checking Question 5?
Big question: why does Question 5 deserve the longest slot?
lessons.homework: Complete a timed 45-minute Question 5 at home using your plan, then note how long each stage actually took.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a visual clock face with colour-coded slots and extra planning prompts. EAL/international: pre-teach 'notional', 'proofread', 'budget'; allow numbers in digits only. Stretch: design a personal exam routine that includes a breathing pause.

lessons.unit: SC-W: Subject content: writing across the course
lessons.title: Writing for impact: rhetorical and creative techniques
lessons.bigQuestion: Which techniques make a reader stop, feel and remember?
objectives: Identify rhetorical techniques (repetition, rule of three, rhetorical question, direct address)
Use creative techniques (motif, extended metaphor, short sentences) in your own writing
Choose a technique to fit audience and purpose, rather than adding all of them
successCriteria: All: use two techniques accurately in a short piece
Most: explain why each technique has impact
Some: blend rhetorical and creative techniques with control and restraint
lessons.crossCurricular: History: speeches that shaped public opinion
lessons.smsc: Moral: using the power of words responsibly and truthfully

keywords.def: repeating the same words at the start of clauses
a list of three, also called the rule of three
a question asked for effect, not for an answer
a repeated image or idea that links a text
a metaphor developed across several sentences

starter: Bismillah. Turn this plain sentence into one with impact: 'It was a quiet night.'
Name one technique that could be used in a speech.
Retrieval: what does 'audience' mean in a writing task?

teach.heading: Two toolkits

left.title: Rhetorical (persuading)
points: Repetition and anaphora
Rule of three (tricolon)
Rhetorical questions
Direct address: 'you'

right.title: Creative (describing, narrating)
points: Motif and symbolism
Extended metaphor
Short sentences for shock
Shifts in focus or time

teach.note: Explain that Subject Content for writing expects pupils to use rhetorical and creative techniques for impact across both papers. Techniques overlap: a motif can persuade; a rhetorical question can build suspense. Ask: where have you seen the rule of three in advertising?

teach.heading: A public-domain model

quote.text: ... government of the people, by the people, for the people, shall not perish from the earth.

teach.note: Point out the repeated 'of the people, by the people, for the people', which is both anaphora and a tricolon. This is public-domain text. Ask: what does the repetition make the audience feel? (Unity, dignity, rhythm.) Note it is a speech, so the sound matters.

teach.heading: Model: from plain to powerful

model.problem: Rewrite for impact for a school assembly speech on kindness: 'We should be kind to each other at school.'
steps: Add a rhetorical question that makes the audience reflect.
Use a tricolon to build rhythm.
Add direct address so the audience feels included.
End on a short, memorable sentence.
model.answer: Who here has never needed a kind word? Kindness costs us nothing: a smile, a shared seat, a gentle hello. You hold that power every single day. Use it.

teach.note: Break down each sentence aloud: the question, the tricolon (a smile, a shared seat, a gentle hello), the direct address 'You', the imperative 'Use it.' Ask pupils to read it as an assembly, feeling the impact. Original model written for TGA.

teach.heading: Creative impact in narrative

model.problem: Open a narrative using a motif and an extended metaphor. Subject: waiting for results.
steps: Pick a repeated image: a clock.
Build a metaphor in 2 to 3 sentences.
Use one very short sentence for emphasis.
Return to the motif at the end.
model.answer: The clock on the wall was a patient judge. Each tick weighed another minute against me. Tick. Tick. Outside, the corridor filled with footsteps, and the judge went on ticking.

teach.note: Name the motif (the clock), the extended metaphor (judge) and the fragment 'Tick. Tick.' as a deliberate short sentence. Stress that the ending returns to the clock, which delivers cohesion. Original model written for TGA.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which choice is best for impact in a narrative about the sea?
options: Using five different techniques in one paragraph
Repeating one motif of waves and using a short sentence for the climax
Using a rhetorical question in every sentence
check.why: Controlled use of one motif plus a short sentence creates a deliberate effect; piling on techniques weakens impact.

teach.note: Mini-whiteboards. Introduce 'less is more': one technique used well beats a list used badly.

practice: Write a tricolon about your favourite season.
Turn 'Pollution is a problem' into a rhetorical question.
Choose a motif and write two sentences that repeat it.
independent: Core: Write a four-sentence speech opening that uses direct address and a tricolon.
Extend: Write a six-sentence narrative paragraph with a motif and one short sentence.
Stretch: Write one paragraph that mixes a rhetorical question and an extended metaphor, then annotate the impact.
exit: Name two rhetorical techniques and one creative technique.
Write one sentence with anaphora.
Big question: which technique had the most impact in your writing today, and why?
lessons.homework: Write a 120-word speech or story opening on a topic you care about, using at least two techniques, and annotate them.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a technique mat with examples and a partly completed model. EAL/international: pre-teach 'tricolon', 'motif', 'patient judge', 'rhetorical'; give sentence frames: 'Who ...?', 'We will ..., we will ..., we will ...'. Stretch: analyse the impact of the Lincoln line on three levels (sound, meaning, audience).

model.problem: Compare the writers' ideas about the sea
steps: Introduction: Both value the sea, but B sees an endless gift, A a dying victim.
Point: they disagree about human power over the sea.
Evidence A: 'treating the sea as a bin'
Evidence B: 'no labour of man could ever empty it'
Comparison: B thinks humans are too small to harm it; A thinks we are harming it already
model.answer: An integrated paragraph.

teach.heading: Hinge
teach.note: Poll.

check.q: Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Both texts are about the sea.
Their views differ because Text B wrote before industrial fishing and plastic, whereas Text A sees the results.
check.why: It synthesises and explains the difference.

practice.q: Write your introduction in two sentences.
practice.a: Both writers value the sea; however, Text B sees an inexhaustible gift, whereas Text A sees a victim of human carelessness.
practice.model: Sentence 1: what they share. Sentence 2: the central difference, with 'whereas'.

practice.q: Plan one integrated paragraph on 'human power over the sea'.
practice.a: Point, evidence from both, comparison.

independent.q: Core: in the portal response box, write the introduction, two integrated paragraphs and a conclusion: 'Compare how the writers present their ideas about the sea.' Starter: 'Both writers...'
independent.a: A full integrated comparison with evidence from both texts.
independent.model: Both writers value the sea, yet they see its future very differently. Text B believes humans are too small to harm it, as 'no labour of man could ever empty it', whereas Text A argues we are already doing so by 'treating the sea as a bin'. Ultimately, the difference reflects their times: one writes before industrial fishing and plastic, the other amid their consequences.

independent.q: Extend: check each paragraph names both texts.
independent.a: All paragraphs integrated.

independent.q: Stretch: comment on the difference in form (letter and article).
independent.a: The private letter is reflective; the public article persuades.

exit.a: For example: Text A 'warning', Text B 'wonder'.

lessons.homework: Redraft your conclusion to include context.
lessons.send: SEND: paragraph frame. EAL: connective bank. Stretch: add a third paragraph on tone.

starter.q: 'Treating the sea as a bin' is...

teach.heading: Two metaphors, two worlds
teach.note: Compare.

left.title: Text A
points: 'a bin': waste, contempt
plain, modern register

right.title: Text B
points: 'a storehouse': plenty, order
formal, elaborate register

teach.heading: Methods table
teach.note: Fill together.

teach.heading: Model: a methods comparison
teach.note: Labelled.

model.problem: Compare how the writers use imagery
steps: A: 'drift like ghosts', death and haunting
B: 'silver harvests', wealth and plenty
Comparison: death against life
Effect on view: A mourns, B celebrates
model.answer: Text A's simile of bags that 'drift like ghosts' makes the sea a place of death, whereas Text B's 'silver harvests' make it a source of wealth, so their imagery mirrors opposite views.

teach.heading: Hinge
teach.note: Poll.

check.q: Text A's 'we' (rather than 'I' or 'you') makes the reader...
check.why: Inclusive 'we' draws the reader into shared guilt and action.

practice.q: Explain Text A's choice of 'we'.
practice.a: It includes the reader in the problem and the solution.
practice.model: Pronoun: we. Effect: shared responsibility, harder to deny. Purpose: persuade to act.

practice.q: Explain Text B's choice of 'I am persuaded'.
practice.a: Personal certainty; the voice of private conviction.

independent.q: Core: in the portal response box, write a comparative paragraph: 'Compare how the writers use language to convey their views.' Starter: 'Both writers use imagery, but...'
independent.a: An integrated paragraph comparing two methods with evidence and effect.
independent.model: Both writers use imagery, but to opposite ends. Text B's metaphor of a 'generous storehouse' presents the sea as orderly and endless, whereas Text A's 'bin' reduces it to a dump for waste. Where Text B's formal register expresses calm wonder, Text A's plain, inclusive 'we' presses the reader to act.

independent.q: Extend: add a sentence on register.
independent.a: Formal and elaborate versus plain and direct.

independent.q: Stretch: which method is most persuasive and why?
independent.a: Answers vary.

exit.a: A metaphor can be more persuasive when it creates a strong, memorable picture.

lessons.homework: Find one metaphor in an article and explain how it conveys a view.
lessons.send: SEND: methods table partly filled. EAL: method glossary. Stretch: compare sentence forms.

teach.heading: Two structures
teach.note: Compare.

left.title: Text A
points: opens with a juxtaposition of clear and choked waters
ends with a conditional warning

right.title: Text B
points: opens with a personal address and place
ends with a sweeping, confident claim

teach.heading: Why endings matter
bullets: The last line stays with the reader
A warning pushes to action
A claim confirms a belief
teach.note: Endings reveal purpose.

teach.heading: Model: comparing structure
teach.note: Labelled.

model.problem: Compare how the writers end
steps: A ends: 'we should not be surprised when it stops feeding us'
Structure: a conditional warning
B ends: 'no labour of man could ever empty it'
Structure: a confident generalisation
Comparison: A looks to a feared future; B rests in present certainty
model.answer: Text A closes with a conditional warning that points to a dangerous future, whereas Text B ends on a confident generalisation that settles the reader in present security.

teach.heading: Hinge
teach.note: Poll.

check.q: Why does Text A open with two contrasting dives?
options: To show loss through a before-and-after juxtaposition
check.why: The juxtaposition sets up the argument.

practice.q: Name Text A's ending structure and its effect.
practice.a: Conditional warning: it makes the reader imagine consequences.
practice.model: 'If we keep..., we should not be surprised...': if-then. Effect: a consequence the reader must avoid.

practice.q: How does Text B's opening address shape tone?
practice.a: 'My dear Sister' creates intimacy and warmth.

independent.q: Core: in the portal response box, write a comparative paragraph: 'Compare how the writers structure their texts to convey their views.' Starter: 'The writers structure their texts very differently:...'
independent.a: An integrated paragraph comparing openings and endings with effect.
independent.model: The writers structure their texts very differently: Text A opens by juxtaposing clear and 'choked' waters, then builds to a conditional warning, whereas Text B begins with an intimate address and flows towards a confident claim. Where Text A's structure pushes readers towards action, Text B's settles them in admiration.

independent.q: Extend: comment on sentence length at the end of each.
independent.a: Text A's measured, final warning; Text B's long, rolling sentence.

independent.q: Stretch: how does form (article and letter) shape structure?
independent.a: Articles argue towards action; letters share feelings with one reader.

exit.a: Purpose: the article persuades, the letter shares.

lessons.homework: Compare the openings of two articles on the same topic.
lessons.send: SEND: structure map. EAL: structural glossary. Stretch: add audience impact.
